results.name: lag1_rating_agreement
results.description: Proportion of consecutive trials (trial_index increasing by 1, same set) with the same yes/no answer; observed above the null means sequential response perseveration (or per-set stickiness) the trial-independent model lacks, below means alternation.

results.name: near_vs_mid_distance_gradient
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 16-30 away; observed below the null means people's generalization falls off with distance more shallowly than the model's interval/rule mixture predicts (above = steeper).
results.code:
# name: near_vs_mid_distance_gradient
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets 16-30 away; observed below the null means people's generalization falls off with distance more shallowly than the model's interval/rule mixture predicts (above = steeper).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values[:, None]
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = (d >= 1) & (d <= 3)
    b = (d >= 16) & (d <= 30)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: inside_range_yes_rate_four_examples
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets lying strictly between the min and max of a four-example set; observed below the null means the model over-generalizes to the spanned interval on rich sets (above = under-generalizes).
results.code:
# name: inside_range_yes_rate_four_examples
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets lying strictly between the min and max of a four-example set; observed below the null means the model over-generalizes to the spanned interval on rich sets (above = under-generalizes).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    notin = ~(ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = (n == 4) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & notin
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: parity_congruence_effect
results.description: Among sets (n>=2) whose examples all share parity, yes rate for non-example targets of the same parity minus those of opposite parity; observed above the null means people use parity more than the model's weighted odd/even rules allow (below = less).
results.code:
# name: parity_congruence_effect
# description: Among sets (n>=2) whose examples all share parity, yes rate for non-example targets of the same parity minus those of opposite parity; observed above the null means people use parity more than the model's weighted odd/even rules allow (below = less).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(ex), 2), np.nan)
    allodd = (np.nansum(par, axis=1) == n)
    alleven = (np.nansum(par, axis=1) == 0)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    notin = ~(ex == t[:, None].astype(float)).any(axis=1)
    same = (allodd & (t % 2 == 1)) | (alleven & (t % 2 == 0))
    base = (n >= 2) & (allodd | alleven) & notin
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = base & same; b = base & ~same
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: set_size_one_two_vs_four_yes_diff
results.description: Yes rate on 1-2 example sets minus yes rate on 4-example sets (non-example targets); observed above the null means people generalize more broadly from few examples / tighten less with more examples than the model's size principle implies (below = they tighten more).
results.code:
# name: set_size_one_two_vs_four_yes_diff
# description: Yes rate on 1-2 example sets minus yes rate on 4-example sets (non-example targets); observed above the null means people generalize more broadly from few examples / tighten less with more examples than the model's size principle implies (below = they tighten more).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    notin = ~(ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = (n <= 2) & notin
    b = (n == 4) & notin
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets more than 30 away from every example; observed above the model's null means people say yes to remote targets more than the model's concepts (plus noise) allow, i.e. a baseline lapse/guess rate is missing.

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples; observed below the model's null means the model is over-confident (lacks lapses/doubt) on exact example targets.

results.name: trial_index_late_minus_early
results.description: Yes rate on trials with trial_index >= 225 minus yes rate on trials < 225; the model has no drift, so observed far from the null means responding to identical stimuli changes over the session (negative = growing conservatism).
